analysis.title: Q3 2026 Global Markets Survey
key_insights: The survey had 460 responses worldwide, collected September 28 to October 1, 2026, during an ongoing bond selloff.
Respondents ranked inflation fears, fiscal fears and stronger-than-expected US growth as the top drivers of the rise in US Treasury yields. 30% picked inflation as the single most important driver.
Deutsche Bank notes the inflation explanation is inconsistent with market pricing, because 10-year US breakevens have hardly moved in the selloff.
Survey 5-year US inflation expectations are 2.9%, up only marginally from 2.8% in June. Euro area 5-year expectations are unchanged at 2.4%.

Respondents expect the 10-year Treasury yield to peak higher over the next 12 months. The average expected peak is 5.70%, versus a recent intraday peak of 5.22%. Most expect about 5.5%, with a secondary cluster around 6%.

On how the US ultimately handles its debt, respondents ranked muddling through indefinitely first, then inflating it away, then stronger growth. Fiscal consolidation ranks near the bottom, and only default ranks lower, overwhelmingly so.

Brent is expected to end the year at an average $95.9/bbl, with about 68% of respondents below $100. Brent started the year near $60, peaked near $120 during the Iran conflict and has recently been around $105.
Ahead of the November 3 US midterms, 82% say the vote raises the US administration's incentive to reach a deal with Iran, while 54% say it lowers Iran's incentive.
82% of respondents put the probability of a US-Iran ceasefire or peace deal before the midterms at 50% or less.
Expectations of AI-driven net job displacement over the next 5 years fell from 67% in March to 52% in September. The beyond-5-years figure is stable at about 55%.
Expectations for generative AI's productivity impact have stabilised, with the largest effect still expected over the longer term. Less than 1% expect no positive impact on growth.
AI use at work keeps rising. Only 2% have not used AI tools for work, versus 8% in March and 14% last December. 'Extensively used' rose from 18% to 39% since December.
Average 12-month US recession probability is 24.7%, up slightly from 24.5% in June and near survey lows. Most respondents sit in the 10-30% range.

Bubble-risk scores (0 to 10) rose in several assets since June. The Magnificent Seven are at 6.9 (from 6.8) and Bitcoin at 6.4 (from 5.7). Bubble-risk scores for US and European credit spreads also rose, with the US back at December 2025 levels. European and non-US tech equities have the lowest perceived risk.

Despite the higher bubble scores, 47% of respondents would hold US equities as their only asset for 10 years. Non-US developed equities are next at 12%, emerging market equities at 10% and gold at 9%. Bitcoin gets 2%.

macro_indicators.indicator: 10-year US Treasury yield, expected 12-month peak (survey average)
macro_indicators.interpretation: Respondents expect yields to go higher than the 5.22% recent intraday peak, with most near 5.5% and a secondary cluster near 6%.

macro_indicators.indicator: 10-year US Treasury yield, most recent intraday peak
macro_indicators.interpretation: Described as a multi-decade high reached in September.
Up only from 2.8% in June, which undercuts the view that inflation is the main driver of the bond selloff.

macro_indicators.indicator: US recession probability, next 12 months (survey average)
macro_indicators.interpretation: Edged up from 24.5% in June and remains near survey lows.
Below the recent level of about $105, with about 68% of respondents expecting under $100.

crypto_views: Bitcoin bubble-risk perception rose to 6.4 from 5.7 in June, a larger rise than the Magnificent Seven's.
Only 2% of respondents would choose Bitcoin as their sole 10-year asset.
risk_factors: Further rise in US 10-year yields: the average respondent expects a peak of 5.70%.
Fiscal fears and US debt sustainability: respondents see muddling through or inflating the debt away as more likely than fiscal consolidation.
Oil and Iran: Brent was around $105 and a deal before the midterms is seen as 50% or less likely by 82% of respondents.
Bubble-risk perception is rising in the Magnificent Seven, Bitcoin and credit spreads.
AI-related net job displacement remains expected by about 52% over 5 years and about 55% beyond 5 years.
vol_and_positioning: Technical factors (positioning and hedging flows) were one of the listed drivers of the Treasury selloff. The text does not state where respondents ranked it.
geopolitical: Iran conflict: Brent peaked near $120 and has recently been around $105.
US midterm elections on November 3: 82% say they raise the US administration's incentive to make a deal with Iran, and 54% say they reduce Iran's incentive.
82% of respondents put the probability of a US-Iran ceasefire or peace deal before the midterms at 50% or less.

theme_stances.key_argument: The popular narrative that inflation is driving the Treasury selloff does not match long-term inflation expectations, which barely moved.
theme_stances.evidence: it doesn’t stack up with long-term inflation expectations
